### Links to the data sources and reproduction of the data selection

**1) The Official Geopgraphic Code (COG), INSEE**

<https://www.insee.fr/fr/information/8740222> ---> The page offers several files. We downloaded and  the CSV file *Liste des communes* as `m_vmt_commune_2026.csv` and renamed `cog_2026`.

**2) COG correspondence table, INSEE** 

<https://www.insee.fr/fr/information/7671867> ---> We downloaded the file *Table de passage annuelle 2026*.

**3) Historical municipal populations, INSEE**

<https://www.insee.fr/fr/statistiques/3698339> ---> We downloaded the XLSX file and exported the first sheet, which contains the population data, as a semicolon-separated CSV file, saved as `population_historique.csv`.

**4) ARCEP fiber deployment**

<https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/le-marche-du-haut-et-tres-haut-debit-fixe-deploiements/> ---> We downloaded the file `2026t2-obs-hd-thd-deploiement-vf.xlsx` (second quarter of 2026) and kept only the sheet *Communes*. 

**5) List of train stations**

<https://www.data.gouv.fr/datasets/liste-des-gares?resource_id=d22ba593-90a4-4725-977c-095d1f654d28>  

**6) Employment of active residents, INSEE**

<https://www.insee.fr/fr/statistiques/4515500> ---> Downloaded the CSV file *Emploi - population active en 2017 - Commune - France hors Mayotte* and kept the municipality code and the number of employed residents aged 15–64 by socio-professional category (variables `C17_ACTOCC1564...`).

**7) Real estate indicators by municipality and by year (prices and volumes for the 2014–2024 period)**

- <https://www.data.gouv.fr/datasets/indicateurs-immobiliers-par-commune-et-par-annee-prix-et-volumes-sur-la-periode-2014-2024?resource_id=084be72a-f586-47f7-92e6-02245e835934> (2019)

- <https://www.data.gouv.fr/datasets/indicateurs-immobiliers-par-commune-et-par-annee-prix-et-volumes-sur-la-periode-2014-2024?resource_id=0350f9a1-04ba-4eb1-9637-d642c9d367d7> (2022)

- <https://www.data.gouv.fr/datasets/indicateurs-immobiliers-par-commune-et-par-annee-prix-et-volumes-sur-la-periode-2014-2024?resource_id=d7881695-1cb5-44c1-900c-00c7158ab766> (2023)

**8) Business' and their establishment, SIRENE**

<https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/base-sirene-des-entreprises-et-de-leurs-etablissements-siren-siret/> ---> Downloaded the file *Sirene : Fichier StockEtablissement – 01 novembre 2026 (format parquet)* and counted the establishments created in each municipality and year since 2014.



## Description of the sources

All the data used in this project are open and freely downloadable without any registration. They are primarily provided from French public institutions such as INSEE, ARCEP and SNCF, and are accessible through the data.gouv.fr platform. The sources differ in time coverage and units of observation. To ensure the geographical consistency across sources, we cleaned and harmonised the data using commune codes.

INSEE (Institut national de la statistique et des études économiques) is the French national statistical institute, responsible for the production and analysis of official statistics in France. It provides four of our datasets:

- The Official Geographic Code (COG) lists all of the French communes with their official codes and names as of 1 January 2026. As some communes have merged or changed code over the years of our study, we also use INSEE’s COG correspondence tables in order to harmonise all sources to one consistent geography.

- Historical data series of municipal populations lets us measure population growth in French communes before and after COVID-19. Since the census has been conducted as a rolling survey in recent years, figures for consecutive years are not independent, so comparisons should use years several years apart.

- “Activité des résidents” describes the occupation sector and the activity of residents in each commune before COVID-19 pandemic. We use it to measure the share of teleworkable occupations, which is one of the indicators of a commune’s suitability for remote work.

ARCEP is the French regulatory authority in charge of regulating telecommunications, postal services and print media distribution in France. It provides the dataset on fixed broadband deployment, which gives the number of premises connectable to fibre in each commune at the end of 2019. The quality of digital infrastructure is used as our second indicator of remote work suitability.
For our third indicator of remote work suitability, we use the list of train stations, provided by SNCF. The quality of the transport infrastructure is identified through communes with rail road access.

The real estate market is captured by the dataset “Indicateurs immobiliers par commune et par année”. This dataset contains property transaction records for each year from 2014 to 2024, and provides information such as property transfer dates, sale values and average price per square meter of properties sold. In our project, we work on three years: 2019 as the pre-pandemic reference, 2022 and 2023 as the post-pandemic period. This allows us to study the evolution of housing prices at the municipal level after the COVID-19 pandemic.

The business creation dataset provided by SIRENE lists all of the French establishments with their creation date and their commune code. We use this data to count the establishments created in each commune over different periods to obtain a measure of local economic dynamism before and after the pandemic.

## Data cleaning

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
```

### Municipality codes

```{r}
cog <- read_csv("data/cog_table_passage_2026.csv", col_types = cols(.default = "c")) |>
  filter(NIVGEO == "COM")

cog_map <- cog |>
  select(starts_with("CODGEO_")) |>
  pivot_longer(-CODGEO_2026, names_to = "year", values_to = "old_code",
               names_prefix = "CODGEO_") |>
  bind_rows(cog |> transmute(CODGEO_2026, year = "2026", old_code = CODGEO_2026)) |>
  filter(!is.na(old_code)) |>
  arrange(desc(year)) |>
  distinct(old_code, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  select(old_code, code_2026 = CODGEO_2026)

nrow(cog_map)
n_distinct(cog_map$code_2026)
```

### Census 2017

```{r}
rp2017 <- read_csv("data/rp2017_emploi_commune.csv", col_types = cols(.default = "c")) |>
  mutate(across(starts_with("C17"), as.numeric))

telework_2017 <- rp2017 |>
  inner_join(cog_map, by = c("CODGEO" = "old_code")) |>
  group_by(code_2026) |>
  summarise(employed_2017 = sum(C17_ACTOCC1564),
            managers_interm_2017 = sum(C17_ACTOCC1564_CS3 + C17_ACTOCC1564_CS4)) |>
  mutate(telework_index = if_else(employed_2017 > 0,
                                  managers_interm_2017 / employed_2017, NA_real_))

rp2017 |> anti_join(cog_map, by = c("CODGEO" = "old_code")) |> nrow()
summary(telework_2017$telework_index)
```

### ARCEP fibre

```{r}
fibre <- read_csv("data/arcep_fibre_communes.csv", col_types = cols(.default = "c"))

fibre_2019 <- fibre |>
  transmute(code = `Code commune`,
            premises_2026 = as.numeric(`Meilleure estimation des locaux T2 2026`),
            fibre_premises_2019 = as.numeric(`T4 2019`)) |>
  inner_join(cog_map, by = c("code" = "old_code")) |>
  group_by(code_2026) |>
  summarise(premises_2026 = sum(premises_2026),
            fibre_premises_2019 = sum(fibre_premises_2019)) |>
  mutate(fibre_share_2019 = if_else(premises_2026 > 0,
                                    pmin(fibre_premises_2019 / premises_2026, 1), NA_real_))

fibre |> anti_join(cog_map, by = c("Code commune" = "old_code")) |> nrow()
summary(fibre_2019$fibre_share_2019)
```

### SIRENE

```{r}
sirene <- read_csv("data/sirene_creations_by_municipality_year.csv",
                   col_types = cols(codeCommuneEtablissement = "c",
                                    year = "i", n_creations = "i"))

arm_map <- tibble(
  old_code = c(sprintf("751%02d", 1:20), sprintf("6938%d", 1:9), sprintf("132%02d", 1:16)),
  code_2026 = c(rep("75056", 20), rep("69123", 9), rep("13055", 16))
)
sirene_map <- bind_rows(cog_map, arm_map)

sirene_clean <- sirene |>
  filter(year <= 2025) |>
  inner_join(sirene_map, by = c("codeCommuneEtablissement" = "old_code")) |>
  group_by(code_2026, year) |>
  summarise(n_creations = sum(n_creations), .groups = "drop")

sirene |>
  anti_join(sirene_map, by = c("codeCommuneEtablissement" = "old_code")) |>
  summarise(unmatched_codes = n_distinct(codeCommuneEtablissement),
            creations_lost = sum(n_creations))

sirene |>
  anti_join(sirene_map, by = c("codeCommuneEtablissement" = "old_code")) |>
  group_by(codeCommuneEtablissement) |>
  summarise(creations = sum(n_creations)) |>
  arrange(desc(creations)) |>
  head(10)
```

### Summary of the cleaning and matching

All sources are linked through the INSEE municipality code. Because French municipalities frequently merge, a code that existed in one year may no longer exist in another. Using the COG correspondence table, we built a list linking every municipality code that existed since 2003 (36716 codes) to its code in 2026 geography (34876 municipalities). Each source was then converted to 2026 codes and the values of merged municipalities were added together.

For the 2017 census data, 45 codes could not be matched. These were the districts of Paris, Lyon and Marseille, which were listed separately even though the data also included the three cities as a whole. We therefore removed them. The remote-work index could not be calculated for 102 municipalities because they had no declared employed residents.

For ARCEP fiber data, only 4 codes could not be matched. AT the end of 2019, more than half of the municipalities had no premises connected to fiber. This means that the fiber shared is often zero. For this reason, we could also use a simple indicator showing whether fiber was available or not.

In the SIRENE data , establishments in Paris, Lyon and Marseille were identified by district. We assigned these districts to their respective cities to make the data consistent with the other sources. The other unmatched codes, representing around 27986new establishments, belong to overseas territories that are not included in the COG municipality list. These territories were excluded from the study. 
Finally, we removed 2026, because the data for this year is incomplete.

## Main variables

- `code_2026`: the INSEE code of municipality in 2026. This code is used to connect all the date from different sources.
- `employed_2017`: the number of people aged 15 to 64 who had a job in the municipality in 2017.
- `managers_interm_2017`: the number of employed people who were managers or had intermediate-level jobs in 2017. These types of jobs are more likely to allow remote work.
- `telework_index`: the percentage of employed people who were managers or had intermediate-level jobs in 2017. It shows how suitable the municipality was for remote work before the pandemic.
- `premises_2026`: the estimated total number of premises (homes and business buildings) in the municipality, according to ARCEP.
- `fibre_premises_2019`: the number of premises that had access to fiber broadband at the end of 2019.
- `fibre_share_2019`: the percentage of premises that could access fiber broadband in 2019. It shows how easy it was to work remotely from that municipality before the pandemic.
- `year`: the year when we establishments were created, between 2014 and 2025.
- `n_creations`: the number of the new establishments created in the municipality each year, based on data from the SIRENE register.

## Research question

Did small French municipalities that were better suited to remote work before the pandemic experience stronger population growth, faster housing price increases and more business creation after COVID-19 than otherwise comparable municipalities?

The COVID-19 pandemic significantly changed the way many people work. During the 2020 lockdowns, employees and companies realised that a large number of jobs could be done remotely. As a result, remote and hybrid work became more common, even after pandemic. This change may have influenced people's decisions about where to live. Since employees no longer have to commute every day, smaller towns and rural areas may have become more attractive because of lower housing costs, more space and a better quality of life. This also raised the question of whether people started leaving large cities, especially Paris, in favour of smaller municipalities.

However, population growth in smaller municipalities cannot automatically be linked to remote work. Some areas were already experiencing demographic changes before the pandemic. Therefore, this study examines whether municipalities that were better suited to remote work before 2020 experienced stronger changes after the pandemic.

We measure the suitability for remote work using two indicators. The first is the share of managers and intermediate-level workers in the 2017 census, as these occupation are generally more likely to allow remote work. The second is the fiber broadband availability at the end of 2019, since a reliable internet connection is essential for working remotely. Both indicator refer to the period before the pandemic, which allows us to avoid measuring changes caused by COVID-19.

The analysis focuses on three outcomes. First, population growth, to understand whether these municipalities attracted more residents. Second, changes in housing prices measured by the median price per square meter, to identify possible increases in housing demand. Third, the number of new establishments created each year, to examine whether remote work may have contributed to local economic activity.

The study focuses on municipalities with fewer that 10000 inhabitants in mainland France. We compare the pre-pandemic period(2014-2018) with the post-pandemic period (2021-2025), excluding 2020 as transition year. We also control for differences between municipalities, including population size, regional trends, rural or urban characteristics and distance from large cities.

This research is relevant for a public policy perspective. If remote work helped smaller municipalities attract residents and businesses, investments in broadband infrastructure and transport could support the development of rural areas. However, increased housing demand could also lead to higher prices, making these municipalities less affordable for their existing residents.

## Graphs

### Business creations

```{r}
#| message: false
library(ggplot2)

sirene_groups <- sirene_clean |>
  inner_join(telework_2017, by = "code_2026") |>
  filter(!is.na(telework_index)) |>
  mutate(telework_group = if_else(telework_index >= median(telework_index),
                                  "High telework index", "Low telework index")) |>
  group_by(year, telework_group) |>
  summarise(n_creations = sum(n_creations), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(sirene_groups, aes(x = year, y = n_creations, colour = telework_group)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Business creations by year and remote-work suitability",
       x = "Year", y = "Number of establishments created", colour = "")
```
